strengths: Novel and timely exploration of 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) as a native visual substrate for vision-language alignment, offering an alternative to standard patch-based pixel tokenization.

Comprehensive systems and algorithmic contributions: structured grid initialization, luminance-aware L1 pruning, and batched CUDA kernels that deliver substantial throughput improvements (up to 90x speedup over existing 2DGS fitting baselines).

Solid empirical evaluation on a 12.8M DataComp subset across all 38 datasets in the CLIP benchmark, showing that 2DGS representations can retain 90–98% of RGB baseline performance under 3×–23.5× compression.

Extensive diagnostic and ablation studies in the appendix, including investigations into stem architectures (Perceiver vs. Point Transformer vs. convolution), distillation objectives, and scratch training dynamics.
weaknesses: Practical edge-cloud motivation is somewhat weakened by the computational cost of 2DGS fitting. While transmission bandwidth is reduced relative to uncompressed RGB, fitting 2D Gaussians requires iterative gradient descent (several seconds per batch even on high-end GPUs like H100s), which is infeasible on resource-constrained edge devices compared to lightweight codecs like JPEG or WebP.

Strong dependence on RGB distillation: as noted in the ablation studies, training 2DGS encoders from scratch leads to severe performance degradation. The method currently serves as an adapted projection of an RGB teacher rather than an autonomous visual learner.

Evaluation is limited to zero-shot CLIP classification. Despite the introduction and Figure 1 highlighting visual token explosion in autoregressive Visual Language Models (e.g., LLaVA), the paper does not evaluate downstream VLM tasks such as visual question answering or captioning.

Experiments are conducted on a downscaled backbone (ViT-B/16 Small with hidden dimension 512) on 12.8M pairs, leading to relatively modest absolute performance numbers (e.g., ~18.5% zero-shot accuracy on ImageNet-1K).

strengths: Novel and creative exploratory concept: Investigating 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) as a continuous, spatially adaptive visual substrate for multimodal vision-language pre-training is a refreshing alternative to standard grid-based patch tokenization.

Substantial systems and algorithmic contributions: The batch-parallel CUDA kernel design, structured initialization (grid layout and local color inheritance), and luminance-regularized pruning yield dramatic speedups (up to 90x) and high GPU utilization (~97%), making dataset-scale 2DGS fitting feasible.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Evaluating across 38 datasets from the CLIP benchmark provides a broad perspective on representation transfer, showing that GS-based encoders retain 90–98% of the baseline zero-shot accuracy.

Honest analysis of architectural limitations: The paper openly discusses current bottlenecks, showing ablations on scratch training, distillation objectives, tokenizer designs, and distribution shifts.
weaknesses: Questionable edge-cloud motivation: The premise centers on reducing edge-to-cloud transmission and energy overhead. However, fitting 2DGS requires iterative per-image optimization (hundreds or thousands of iterations), which would impose immense compute and battery drain on resource-constrained edge devices compared to standard image codecs like JPEG or WebP.

Misleading compression baseline: Compression ratios (3x–23.5x) and loading speedups are calculated against uncompressed raw RGB pixels (224x224x3 bytes). In real-world edge-cloud pipelines, raw uncompressed images are never transmitted; JPEG or WebP compression routinely achieves 10x–30x compression with negligible encoding latency and competitive file sizes (e.g., 2–5 KB per 224x224 image vs. 6.4 KB for 400 FP16 Gaussians).

Token reduction is driven by the Perceiver resampler rather than 2DGS itself: The reduction from 196 to 98 visual tokens is achieved through the Perceiver cross-attention stem, a technique equally applicable to raw pixel patches. As shown in Table 7, fine-tuning the RGB ViT baseline with 98 tokens achieves 20.56% average accuracy, outperforming all 98-token GS models.

Heavy reliance on RGB distillation: Training 2DGS models from scratch fails to converge effectively (Figure 21). The framework strictly requires pre-distilling features from an RGB-pretrained teacher ViT, meaning the representation is fundamentally bound and capped by existing pixel-based inductive biases rather than developing native multimodal representations from Gaussians.

Sub-baseline overall accuracy: Experiments use a reduced-capacity ViT-B/16 (Small) with a 512 hidden dimension trained on a 12.8M DataComp subset, yielding modest baseline zero-shot performance (22.20% average, 18.51% on ImageNet-1k). It remains uncertain how well these conclusions transfer to standard full-scale CLIP backbones (e.g., ViT-B/16 with 768 width, ViT-L/14) and larger datasets.

strengths: Novel Conceptual Exploration: The paper tackles an unconventional and creative research question—investigating whether 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) can act as an alternative, compact visual representation directly consumable by vision-language models (CLIP) rather than relying on standard patchified pixel grids.

Substantial Engineering and Systems Effort: The authors develop custom batched CUDA kernels, structured grid initialization, and luminance-aware L1 pruning, demonstrating up to 90x speedup over existing 2DGS fitting codebases and enabling the fitting of a large-scale multimodal dataset (12.8M images from DataComp).

Extensive Empirical Evaluation: The method is evaluated across 38 datasets from the CLIP benchmark across varying Gaussian budgets (400 to 3136 points) and token lengths (98 and 196 tokens), accompanied by extensive ablation studies in the appendix.
weaknesses: Core Motivation Contradiction for Edge-to-Cloud Scenarios: The paper heavily motivates 2DGS by pointing to the transmission energy/bandwidth bottlenecks of sending visual data from edge devices to the cloud. However, fitting 2DGS requires iterative gradient-based optimization (2,000 iterations per image). Running thousands of optimization steps on battery- and compute-constrained edge devices consumes vastly more energy and latency than standard hardware-accelerated image codecs (e.g., JPEG, WebP, AVIF), which encode in single-digit milliseconds with minimal energy. This undermines the practical premise of using 2DGS as an edge-to-cloud transmission substrate.

Unrealistic Compression Baseline: The compression ratios reported in Table 1 (3x to 23.5x) are calculated strictly relative to uncompressed, raw 24-bit RGB pixel arrays (224x224x3 bytes). In real-world transmission and storage, images are virtually always compressed using standard image codecs, which easily achieve 10x-30x compression on 224x224 images without noticeable perceptual degradation. Comparing against raw bytes paints an overly favorable picture of the transmission advantage.

Heavy Dependence on Pretrained RGB Distillation: The 2DGS encoder cannot be trained effectively from scratch (Section 6, Section 11.5, Fig. 21). Instead, it relies fundamentally on feature distillation from a pretrained RGB ViT backbone. This indicates that 2DGS does not provide a self-sufficient representational substrate with strong native inductive biases; rather, it acts primarily as an imperfect approximation/surrogate for an already-learned RGB manifold.

Catastrophic Degradation on Fine-Grained / High-Frequency Domains: While the overall average zero-shot accuracy appears relatively close to the baseline, the representation suffers catastrophic failures on tasks relying on fine-grained, low-contrast, or subtle high-frequency cues. For instance, on Diabetic Retinopathy, accuracy collapses from 38.33% (RGB) to 3.09% (GS-3136), and on FER2013 from 17.41% to 7.19%. This exposes critical representational blind spots inherent to Gaussian-splat approximations.

Low Baseline Performance Level: The baseline used throughout is a non-standard, reduced-width 'ViT-B/16 (Small)' (width 512, 38M params) yielding an absolute zero-shot accuracy of only 22.20% on average (and 18.51% on ImageNet-1k). Because the baseline model is operating at a relatively low performance regime, it remains unproven whether the observations hold for fully converged, competitive production-grade CLIP models (e.g., standard ViT-B/16 or ViT-L/14).

Inconsistencies in Appendix Cross-Referencing: In Section 11.6, references to figures are misaligned (e.g., referencing Figs. 14, 15, and 16 for experiments that correspond to Figures 20, 21, and 22 on page 25).

strengths: Explores an interesting and timely research direction: using 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) as an alternative, compact visual representation directly for vision-language alignment (CLIP), rather than relying on standard pixel grids and post-hoc token pruning.

Presents solid engineering and system-level contributions to make 2DGS fitting scalable, including batched CUDA kernels, structured grid initialization, and luminance-aware pruning, achieving significant throughput gains over previous single-image 2DGS implementations.

Proposes a well-motivated adaptation architecture (GS Stem with Fourier position encodings, log-scaled covariance, gating, and Perceiver Resampler) that allows parameter-efficient transfer from pretrained RGB transformers by freezing ~93% of backbone weights.
weaknesses: Very narrow downstream evaluation: The empirical validation of vision-language alignment is limited solely to zero-shot ImageNet-1K classification. Standard CLIP evaluations require a comprehensive suite of zero-shot transfer benchmarks (e.g., ImageNet variants, CIFAR, downstream fine-grained classification) and image-text retrieval tasks (e.g., MS-COCO, Flickr30k). Without these, it is difficult to determine whether semantic richness and multimodal alignment generalize beyond coarse ImageNet classes.

Weak baseline anchor: The RGB teacher model only achieves 18.5% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K. Operating in this low-accuracy regime makes it unclear whether the relative retention of performance by the 2DGS encoder (13–15%) will hold when scaling to competitive vision-language baselines (which typically exceed 60–75% top-1 zero-shot on ImageNet).

Unsubstantiated edge-cloud efficiency premise: The paper motivates 2DGS as an energy-efficient alternative to RGB transmission for edge devices. However, fitting 2DGS primitives requires iterative gradient descent passes through a differentiable renderer. Running hundreds or thousands of fitting iterations on resource-constrained edge hardware is significantly more compute- and energy-intensive than traditional JPEG/HEVC encoding. The manuscript lacks an end-to-end edge compute, latency, and energy benchmark comparing 2DGS optimization + transmission against standard compression.

Lack of systematic architectural ablations: While the components of the GS Stem (Fourier encoding, log-scale covariance, gated linear layer, Perceiver Resampler vs. simple pooling) are introduced, there are no component-by-component ablation studies demonstrating their individual necessity and empirical contributions to final alignment.

Presentation limitations: In Figure 7, the plots for top-1/top-5 accuracy, contrastive loss, and logit scale are unreadably small, with blurred axis labels and illegible legends, making it difficult to assess the findings from the training-from-scratch experiments.

strengths: Explores a creative and non-standard direction by investigating 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) as a continuous, adaptive visual input representation for contrastive vision-language pre-training (CLIP).

Presents valuable system and engineering optimizations for 2DGS fitting, including batched CUDA kernels, grid-based structured initialization, and luminance-guided L1 pruning, yielding significant throughput gains over previous unbatched baselines.

The parameter-efficient adaptation pipeline (splat-aware GS stem with Fourier positional encoding and Perceiver Resampler, updating only ~7% of parameters) is sensibly designed to leverage pretrained RGB transformer weights.
weaknesses: A fundamental conceptual disconnect exists regarding the edge-to-cloud motivation: Fitting 2DGS requires hundreds or thousands of iterative gradient steps through a differentiable renderer per image. Running this optimization on resource-constrained edge devices would consume far more energy and compute than standard codecs (e.g., JPEG, WebP, HEVC), which encode images in milliseconds on low-power hardware.

The compression comparison is overstated: Compression ratios (3–20×) are computed against raw uncompressed pixel arrays in float16. Standard image codecs easily achieve 10–30× compression with virtually zero compute overhead, making the transmission and bandwidth efficiency claims misleading without a rigorous end-to-end codec comparison.

Experimental evaluation is exceptionally narrow for a CLIP/vision-language alignment submission. The model is evaluated solely on ImageNet-1K zero-shot accuracy, omitting standard benchmarks in the CLIP and DataComp suites (e.g., cross-modal retrieval on Flickr30K/COCO, robustness benchmarks like ImageNet-A/R/V2, and the broader 38-task DataComp evaluation suite).

Absolute classification performance remains weak: The RGB reference model achieves only 18.5% zero-shot top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K (due to reduced ViT width and training scale), and the 2DGS encoder trails this modest baseline further by 3.5–5.5% (achieving 13–15%). Direct pre-training from scratch on 2DGS inputs also fails entirely as shown in Figure 7.

Missing crucial baselines: The paper does not benchmark against existing compressed-domain learning approaches (e.g., training encoders on JPEG DCT coefficients) or patch-level token pruning/merging methods (such as ToMe, PruMerge, or standard Perceiver resamplers on RGB patches) under matched token and transmission budgets.
Figure 7 contains illegible, microscopic axis labels, titles, and legends, making it very difficult to inspect the training curves and comparisons.

strengths: Explores a novel and creative direction by evaluating 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) as a native visual representation for vision-language alignment (CLIP) rather than solely as a graphics reconstruction codec.

Provides valuable engineering and systems contributions, including batched CUDA kernels, structured grid initialization, and luminance-aware L1 pruning, yielding significant fitting acceleration (up to 90x) and high GPU utilization (~97%).

Presents an effective parameter-efficient transfer scheme that reuses frozen RGB-pretrained transformer backbones with a custom Gaussian stem and Perceiver Resampler, updating only ~7% of model parameters.

Demonstrates viable zero-shot classification performance (13–15% top-1 on ImageNet-1K) across varied Gaussian counts and compression ratios compared to an 18.5% RGB teacher baseline trained on a 12.8M DataComp subset.
weaknesses: Narrow empirical evaluation: Validation is restricted solely to ImageNet-1K zero-shot top-1 and top-5 accuracy. Standard vision-language evaluation requires a broader suite of benchmarks (e.g., zero-shot retrieval on Flickr30k/MS-COCO, DataComp 38-dataset evaluation suite, or visual reasoning tasks) to convincingly verify multimodal alignment.

Lack of essential compression baselines: The paper compares 2DGS compression ratios against uncompressed raw pixel arrays (float16 / uncompressed RGB) rather than standard codecs such as JPEG, WebP, or AVIF. At 224x224 resolution, standard JPEG achieves comparable or smaller file sizes (<10 KB) without noticeable degradation. An experiment evaluating RGB CLIP on images compressed with standard codecs at matched bitrates is missing.

Edge-cloud feasibility concern: The primary motivation is reducing transmission energy from edge devices to the cloud. However, fitting 2D Gaussians requires hundreds or thousands of gradient descent iterations through a differentiable renderer. The paper does not benchmark the computational, runtime, or energy overhead of running iterative 2DGS fitting on resource-constrained edge hardware versus standard hardware-accelerated JPEG/video encoding.

Missing ablation studies and numerical tables: The contribution of specific GS stem design choices (Fourier coordinate encodings, log-scaled covariances, gated linear units, and Z-score normalization) is not ablated. Furthermore, the main results in Section 5.2 are reported via small scatter plots (Figure 6) without detailed tabular breakdowns.
